source: Kumar and Schockaert (2023) Solving hard analogy questions with relation embedding chains
finding: GPT-4 (few solved examples plus explanations in the prompt) was run on SAT, U2, U4, BATS, Google, SCAN and E-KAR next to RelBERT. GPT-4 is far ahead on easy lexical sets and not ahead of RelBERT on SAT.
limits: Table 2. No confidence intervals reported. Prompt not tuned. SAT has 374 items, so a 70.3 score has a binomial 95% interval of about +/-4.6 points (derived here, not in the paper).
agent_relevance: Gives a 2023 GPT-4 anchor for gap 3. A strong LLM roughly ties a cheap fine-tuned relation-embedding model (RelBERT) on SAT, so an embedding scorer is a credible low-cost baseline.

source: Kumar and Schockaert (2023) Solving hard analogy questions with relation embedding chains (contamination caveat)
finding: The authors state that GPT-4 may have seen some of these datasets in training, which could inflate its results. They did not test it.
numbers: No contamination test. They also note LLM results are prompt-sensitive.
quote: it is possible that GPT-4 has seen some of the datasets during training, which could lead to inflated results
limits: Statement of risk only. The Yuan 2023 numbers they reuse came from models fine-tuned on validation splits for some methods, so they are not comparable (their footnote 7).
agent_relevance: Contamination of SAT/U2/U4/BATS for GPT-4-class models is acknowledged by a group that ran the benchmark and is still unmeasured (gap 2).

source: Kumar and Schockaert (2023) Solving hard analogy questions with relation embedding chains (confidence stratification)
finding: RelBERT's own informativeness score, conf = min(inf(r_ab), inf(r_xy)) for the query pair and the chosen answer pair, predicts whether its answer is right. Accuracy climbs steadily with the score for RelBERT and also for GPT-4.
numbers: Average over 7 datasets, RelBERT: 31.1% (conf <0.25), 45.5% (0.25-0.5), 58.7% (0.5-0.75), 71.2% (>=0.75). GPT-4 on the same bins: 59.5, 60.6, 65.0, 72.9. SAT RelBERT 40.7 -> 51.4 -> 78.0 -> 80.6; SAT GPT-4 59.3 -> 54.3 -> 65.0 -> 78.3. BATS GPT-4 stays 87-94 in all bins. SCAN is flat for all models (about 19-36).
limits: The score is a learned relation-informativeness measure, not the raw cosine margin between candidates. Bin sizes are not given in the text I read. No calibration curve or abstention precision/recall.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 4. A relation-embedding confidence is a usable difficulty/abstain signal and it also separates GPT-4's hard items. The cosine-margin version for general LLM embeddings is still untested.

source: Kumar and Schockaert (2023) Solving hard analogy questions with relation embedding chains (chains on hard items)
finding: On the hardest bin (RelBERT confidence <0.25), composing relation embeddings along ConceptNet paths beats plain RelBERT on most datasets. Routing only low-confidence items to the chain gives small overall gains.
numbers: Hard bin, average over datasets: RelBERT 31.1, Condensed chain 42.1, Direct chain 44.5, GPT-4 59.5. Overall SAT: RelBERT 73.6, Condensed 70.6, Direct 63.8; hybrids 73.3-74.5 (gain 0 to +0.9). U2: RelBERT 67.5, hybrids Direct<0.25 70.2, Direct<0.5 71.1 (+2.7 to +3.6).
limits: Hybrid gains are within noise on a 374-item SAT. GPT-4 beats every embedding method on the hard bin on average.
agent_relevance: A cheap vector scorer plus a fallback only for low-confidence cases is a sensible shape for an agent. In this study the fallback that won was a bigger model, not another vector method.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (supplement S3, contamination checks)
finding: The authors tried to test whether GPT-3 had memorised their analogy items. For the 374-item SAT set they prompted GPT-3 with only the A and B terms and found no sign of memorisation.
numbers: SAT set: 374 problems, said not to be on the public web but distributed to a small number of researchers. The memorisation probe is qualitative; no numbers.
quote: we were not able to find any evidence that GPT-3 had memorized any of these problems
limits: Probe covers GPT-3 (2022) only. A completion probe can miss partial memory. The same SAT items are now in public datasets (Kumar and Schockaert took them from the RelBERT repository), so this check does not cover GPT-4 or newer models.
agent_relevance: The only memorisation probe for SAT in the record. It is old and weak, so SAT scores of newer models stay possibly contaminated until a fresh-item test exists (gap 2 stays open).

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets are meant to be unlike training data. Humans stay high across alphabets. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 fall as the alphabet is more permuted, which the authors read as reuse of patterns seen in training.
numbers: Table 2 pooled over alphabets: 1,876 human samples and 6,840 per GPT model; accuracies 0.753 [0.734, 0.773], 0.488 [0.467, 0.509], 0.350 [0.330, 0.370], 0.452 [0.431, 0.473]. The first value matches the human result in the text. The mapping of the other three to GPT-3 / GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 comes from a garbled table and stays only moderately certain.
limits: Letter-string tasks, not verbal SAT analogies. Models are 2023 versions. Several alphabets were simple permutations on which models still did fairly well.
agent_relevance: The only perturbation-style test in the record. The same idea (change the surface form, keep the relation) is the right contamination test for SAT and BATS, but nobody has run it on verbal analogies. Supports building perturbed copies of our own agent tests.

source: Freestone and Karmaker Santu (2024) Word embeddings revisited: do LLMs offer something new?
finding: Embedding comparison on BATS with vector-offset analogies. ADA-002 and PaLM 2 embeddings come out best, SBERT often third, LLaMA2-7B worst of the LLM group. Input words are excluded from candidates; top-1 over an 80,000-word WordNet pool.
numbers: Table 1 (BATS; 3CosAdd, 3CosAvg, 3CosMul, LRCos, PairDistance): SBERT 0.243/0.261/0.267/0.487/0.086; USE 0.174/0.212/0.187/0.450/0.025. Row labels are shifted in the extraction. Most likely mapping (inferred from the text ranking): ADA 0.412/0.447/0.424/0.375/0.232; PaLM 2 0.398/0.458/0.417/0.534/0.193; LLaMA2 0.145/0.200/0.145/0.131/0.053; LASER 0.227/0.260/0.237/0.284/0.121.
limits: Offset arithmetic, not multiple-choice SAT. Only 6 models. Authors avoid saying one is better because of the Linzen 2016 and Fournier 2020 critiques. The mean cosine of random word pairs differs strongly across models (Figure 1), so a raw cosine threshold does not transfer between models.
agent_relevance: Modern embeddings still stay below 0.55 on BATS with vector offset (best 0.534 with LRCos), far under the 90.8% of a prompted GPT-4 (d01). For relation matching an agent should prompt a model rather than do offset arithmetic. A cosine threshold must be set per model (gap 4).

source: Petersen and van der Plas (2024) Can language models learn analogical reasoning? Training objectives and comparison to human performance
finding: Untrained BERT, scored by cosine of pair differences, is near chance at telling true from false analogies on human-style sets (SAT, U2, U4, SCAN). Fine-tuning on a small amount of analogy data raises it. The cosine of relation differences is biased by word frequency and out-of-vocabulary words.
numbers: Untrained BERT classification accuracy is about 0.47-0.52 across the SAT/U2/U4/SCAN groups; FastText 0.50-0.57 (it labels almost everything negative). After tuning, groups reach about 0.57-0.82. SAT has almost 30% out-of-vocabulary words, SCAN under 10%. Entities in false analogies appear more often in pretraining than those in true ones; before tuning, items with no OOV words are almost always predicted true.
limits: Table cells were scrambled in extraction, so these are ranges from legible rows, not a full table. BERT-size encoders, not 2025 embedding models.
agent_relevance: Bears on gaps 5 and 7: cosine of relation differences carries a frequency bias, a boundary condition for any cheap relational similarity. Calibrate on items from the agent's own domain.

source: Das and Balke (2025) From prototypical to relational: how LLMs navigate complex analogies (SAT section)
finding: The authors re-ran the 374-item SAT analogy set on LLaMA 2 13B/70B, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o (zero-shot and one-shot with CoT) and compared with encoder results from Petersen and van der Plas. Large decoders beat the human mark by a clear margin. One CoT example helped GPT models only slightly.
numbers: Results are shown only as a bar chart (Figure 3), so no per-model numbers could be read from the text. Text: small decoders match human accuracy and encoders; GPT-4-class models beat humans by a substantial margin.
limits: No numbers in the text, no confidence intervals, and no contamination check although SAT items are public.
agent_relevance: A 2025 confirmation that SAT is saturated for frontier decoders. It cannot tell how much is memorised, so SAT cannot rank agents (gaps 2 and 3).

source: Das and Balke (2025) From prototypical to relational (multi-plausible-answer benchmark)
finding: New 1,210-item four-way analogy set in which every option shares some relation with the stem; the gold answer is set by ranked relational overlap, context-embedding similarity, or prototypicality. Models do well on prototypicality and embedding similarity and poorly on ranked relational overlap.
numbers: Table 2 accuracy, three prompt settings per measure (column names not confirmed in the text). Relational overlap: GPT-4o-mini 29.44/27.62/36.06, GPT-4o 29.03/28.12/25.55, GPT-4.1 24.16/21.33/25.55, Llama3 70B 22.13/28.36/31.15. Embedding similarity: GPT-4.1 48.38/48.13/48.13, GPT-4o 43.92/45.32/44.19. Prototypicality: GPT-4.1 52.85/51.69/52.87, GPT-4o 47.72/47.97/49.13. Chance is 25%.
limits: Row labels at the table bottom are shifted in extraction; I used rows with readable labels. Relation salience labels come from a GPT-4 Max-Diff survey (agreement 0.79 with experts for GPT-4.1), so gold is partly LLM-made. Measures use different gold answers, so columns are not comparable with each other.
agent_relevance: When several relations are plausible, frontier models pick the prototypical or embedding-nearest answer, and score at about 22-36% on the relational measure (close to the 25% chance level). A relation-based retriever must state which relation it wants, or it returns the prototypical neighbour (gaps 6 and 8).

source: Das and Balke (2025) From prototypical to relational (knowledge-enhanced prompting)
finding: Adding a prompt that asks the model to infer and rank the relations of each pair helps open and small models more than the strongest GPT models, and does not fix the relational-overlap weakness.
numbers: Text: relational overlap LLaMA-2 70B 22.1 -> 31.1 (this matches the table row printed as Llama3 70B, so the label is inconsistent); prototypicality Gemma-2B 24.8 -> 36.9, RWKV-1.5B 30.0 -> 35.2; embedding similarity LLaMA-2 13B 28.3 -> 33.8. Authors call the gains marginal and inconsistent.
limits: One dataset, no repeats or intervals. A direct contrast of fixed template versus model-generated relation description was not run.
agent_relevance: Partial evidence for gap 6: an explicit fixed instruction about relations gave gains to weaker models but nothing reliable at the top. Not a test of fixed templates against generated descriptions.

source: Jiayang and others (2023) StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: Sentence embeddings, including OpenAI text-embedding-ada, track entity and relation similarity but do not track the human analogy score. Models built to see relations (DMR discourse relations, RelBERT, noun GloVe) do better at analogy identification.
numbers: 24K story pairs. Abstract: ChatGPT about 30% on the multiple-choice analogy test versus over 85% for humans. ProPara correlation with the analogy score (x100): RoBERTa 6.2, SimCSE 1.8, OpenAI-ada 3.4, DMR 12.6, RelBERT 7.5, human annotators 67.9. The same encoders correlate 35-53 with entity and relation similarity.
quote: suitable for literal similarity retrieval but not analogy retrieval
limits: Story-level text, not word pairs. Table columns were inferred from the printed header after heavy extraction damage. Sentence encoders from 2021-2022, not newer 2025 embedding models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 5 (general embeddings find similar things, not analogous things) and for gap 1: the authors say embeddings suit literal-similarity retrieval but not analogy retrieval.

source: Su and others (2025) BRIGHT: a realistic and challenging benchmark for reasoning-intensive retrieval
finding: Retrieval benchmark where the right document shares the underlying theorem or algorithm with the query, not the topic words (LeetCode, AoPS, TheoremQA-Q: find solved problems using the same theorem). Top embedding models drop from 59.0 nDCG@10 on MTEB to 18.3 here.
numbers: 1,384 queries, 12 task sets. SFR-Embedding-Mistral 18.3 average. BM25 average 14.5; BM25 per set: LeetCode 24.4, Pony 7.9, AoPS 6.2, TheoremQA-Q 10.4, TheoremQA-T 4.9. Qwen embedding LeetCode 25.5, AoPS 14.4, TheoremQA-Q 27.8 (columns read from a partly cut table line). Reranking with GPT-4 top-10 gave 21.5 on one retriever versus 19.5 with no rerank, while a MiniLM reranker gave 16.0.
limits: nDCG@10 for document retrieval, not downstream solving. Gold for same-theorem sets was set by annotators using the shared theorem or algorithm, a stricter relation than most agent tasks. Reranking helped only with strong LLMs.
agent_relevance: Closest existing test of gap 1: retrieving solved problems by shared method rather than shared topic is hard for plain embedding similarity. It does not test a relation-specific embedding, and there is no equal-token agent-level comparison.

source: Su and others (2025) BRIGHT (query rewriting with LLM reasoning)
finding: Rewriting the query as an LLM reasoning trace before retrieval helps. BM25 on GPT-4 reasoning steps becomes the best retriever on the leaderboard. This is the retrieval counterpart of letting a model write the relation description.
numbers: Abstract: explicit reasoning about the query improves retrieval by up to 12.2 points. Figure 3 caption: BM25 with GPT-4 reasoning steps is best. BM25 with the plain query averages 14.5.
limits: Per-set numbers are in appendix tables 34-38, which I did not read. The cost of a GPT-4 generation per query is not matched in tokens against the baselines.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 6 in retrieval form: a model-written description of what the problem needs beat the plain query and the fixed embedding. The price is a model call, not a cheap vector lookup.

source: Yasunaga and others (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (retrieved-CoT baseline)
finding: The retrieved-exemplar baseline picks the top 5 similar training problems by cosine similarity, so it is a whole-text similarity retriever. Self-generated exemplars beat it on strong models and lose to it on weak models.
numbers: GSM8K scale table (Table 4): text-davinci-003 retrieved 54 (a second line reading 57 may belong to this row; the extraction is scrambled) vs self-generated 61; text-davinci-001 retrieved 11 vs self-generated 9; curie-001 2 vs 2. Best self-generated results in Table 1: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo 77.8, davinci-003 61.0, PaLM2 81.7; MATH GPT-3.5-turbo 37.3, PaLM2 34.8, against the next row 76.7 / 54.0 / 80.7 and 34.9 / 34.3.
limits: Self-generation costs more output tokens (first listed limitation), and no equal-token comparison against retrieval is given. Models were accessed June-September 2023.
agent_relevance: Not an equal-token test of relation- versus topic-retrieval, but the nearest: whole-text cosine retrieval is the weaker option once the model can write its own analogues (gaps 1 and 9).

source: Yasunaga and others (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (GPT-4 and limits)
finding: On Codeforces, GPT-4 gains a few points from self-generated exemplars plus knowledge; GPT-3.5-turbo-16k gains a little more in Acc@1. The authors say self-generation can fail if the model is not strong enough.
numbers: Table 2 (Acc@1 / Acc@10), reading rows as 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 3-shot CoT, self-generated exemplars, exemplars+knowledge: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k 8/24, 9/27, 11/27, 13/25, 15/29; GPT-4 16/30, 16/29, 17/31, 17/32, 19/37. So GPT-4 gains +2 Acc@1 and +6 Acc@10 over 3-shot CoT.
quote: self-generation can fail if the LLM lacks sufficient strength
limits: Row order inferred from the printed labels. A 2-point Acc@1 gain on a small set with no intervals may be noise. GPT-4 was the June-September 2023 version. No 2025-26 model tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only partly answered. Authors tie the weak-model failure to missing recall ability, but no one shows the effect holds or grows on current frontier models.

source: Yu, He and Ying (2024) Thought propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs
finding: Instead of retrieving analogues, the LLM proposes and solves a set of analogous problems and reuses their results to fix the first answer. No embedding retrieval is used.
numbers: Abstract: average 12% absolute increase in finding the optimal solution in shortest-path reasoning, 13% better human preference in creative writing, 15% better task completion in LLM-agent planning, over baselines.
limits: Gains are against prompting baselines and cost extra calls (propose, solve, aggregate). Tasks (graphs, household planning) have a well-defined relation between problems, so this is a domain with a gold relation (gap 8 not answered). I read the abstract and method headings, not every table.
agent_relevance: Shows the generated-analogue route, with no vector store, can help agent planning. There is still no head-to-head with relation-embedding retrieval at equal tokens.

source: Petrov and others (2025) ALF: a fine-grained French analogy dataset for evaluating lexical knowledge of LLMs
finding: On English BATS, small instruction models score in the mid-80s, but on ALF (2,600 fine-grained French lexical analogies from Meaning-Text lexical functions) the same models fall to about 50-60%. FastText on ALF is far lower.
numbers: BATS (Table 2, 50 pairs x 40 relations): ChatGPT-4o-mini EM 84.0 (CM 86.0, SM 84.7), with feedback 86.6; Llama3.0-8B and 3.1-8B about 80-86 EM; reference figures quoted: ChatGPT 84.0 (Yuan 2023), GloVe 28.5 (Gladkova 2016). ALF (Table 3): ChatGPT EM 51.11 / CM 55.15; Llama3.0 50.17 / 53.74; Llama3.1 49.49 / 55.49; Qwen2.5-14B 54.00 / 59.66; fastText(fr) 11.92 / 16.00.
limits: BATS rows partly mislabelled in extraction (a Qwen row with 32.2 EM probably belongs to fastText). English BATS versus French ALF mixes language, relation type and exposure, so the drop is not a clean contamination estimate. Paradigmatic lexical functions score higher than syntagmatic ones (one function reaches 91% CM).
agent_relevance: Weak hint for gaps 2 and 7: scores fall by about 30 points when relations are rarer and the items are new and not widely published. The authors also say ChatGPT's BATS score matched Yuan 2023 closely but neither paper gives enough detail to reproduce exactly.
